title: Teaching & Training Design
subtitle: Evidence-based teaching: how people learn, building skill with practice and feedback, and running inclusive sessions.
outcomes: Explain how learners move from novice to expert
Design lessons that respect memory and cognitive load
Create motivating, inclusive and well-managed learning environments

pool.q: Why are practice and feedback so important in a workshop?
options: Because a workshop is not simply a source of information but the starting point for developing a new skill
Because instructors are graded on them
pool.explain: Learners move from novice towards competence by practising and getting feedback.
pool.evidence: a Carpentries workshop is not simply a source of information: It is the starting point for development of a new skill.

pool.q: What is a critical part of building a new skill in a workshop?
options: Practising in real time, getting feedback and applying it to the next step
Listening to a long lecture first
Reading the whole manual before starting
pool.explain: A workshop is the starting point for developing a skill, not just a source of information.
pool.evidence: learners are able to practice what they are learning in real time, get feedback on what they are doing, and then apply those lessons learned to the next step in the learning process

pool.q: What does 'all models are wrong, but some are useful' mean for mental models?
options: Models are imperfect but still helpful
pool.explain: Analogies and concept maps help build useful mental models.
pool.evidence: Models are not perfect but are still helpful

pool.q: Which of these is a common misconception mentioned in the lesson?
options: That the seasons are caused by the shape of Earth's orbit
pool.explain: Misconceptions must be found and corrected, not just added to.
pool.evidence: or that seasons are related to the shape of the earth's orbit

pool.q: What kind of mental model does a competent practitioner have?
options: One that is useful for everyday purposes
pool.explain: Experts have richer, more connected models.
pool.evidence: A competent practitioner has a mental model that is useful for everyday purposes.

pool.q: Why is seeing a novice as an 'empty vessel' a problem?
options: The analogy is inaccurate and can create dangerous misconceptions
pool.explain: Novices already have some (often wrong) mental models.
pool.evidence: Unfortunately, this analogy includes inaccuracies that can generate dangerous misconceptions.

pool.q: What is the problem behind the 'expert awareness gap'?
options: Experts forget that novices need the intermediate steps between ideas
pool.explain: Going from A to F in one leap skips steps B and C that novices need.
pool.evidence: it can be very hard to remember that novices need to go through steps B and C before they can understand the connection between A and F

pool.q: When demonstrating as an expert, what is important?
options: Explaining step by step how each step leads to the next
pool.explain: Make your reasoning visible to learners.
pool.evidence: It is important to explain what you are doing step-by-step, and how each step leads to the next one.

pool.q: What is working memory?
options: The memory you use to actively think about things
pool.explain: Working memory is small, so cognitive load must be managed carefully.
pool.evidence: This is the type of memory you use to actively think about things and is often called working memory.

pool.q: How does long-term memory differ from short-term memory?
options: It is essentially unlimited but slow to access
It forgets everything after a day
pool.explain: Short-term (working) memory is fast but very limited.
pool.evidence: (barring injury or disease, we will die before it fills up) but it is slow to access

pool.q: How can instructors support learners' limited short-term memory?
options: By not flooding it with too many separate pieces of information
By covering as much as possible quickly
By testing only at the end
pool.explain: Going slowly with frequent checks also helps.
pool.evidence: we can support learners by not flooding their short term memory with too many separate pieces of information

pool.q: What is chunking?
options: Splitting a lesson into random parts
Linking separate items so they can be remembered as a single item
pool.explain: Chunks let more information fit in short-term memory.
pool.evidence: or relationships among separate items, allowing them to be remembered as a single item

pool.q: Why should assessments during teaching be frequent?
options: Short-term memory is limited in time as well as space
pool.explain: Frequent checks catch problems before they fade or compound.
pool.evidence: short-term memory is limited not only in space, but also in time

pool.q: What is formative assessment used for during workshops?
options: To track learners' progress and adjust the teaching as needed
To grade learners for a certificate
To rank learners against each other
To decide who may attend the next workshop
pool.explain: Short checks during teaching reveal misunderstandings early.
pool.evidence: We use formative assessment of learners during workshops to help track learners' progress and adjust our approach to teaching the content as needed.

pool.q: Like all other skills, what does good teaching require?
pool.explain: The belief that good teachers are simply born is wrong.
pool.evidence: Like all other skills, good teaching requires practice and feedback.

pool.q: Which two tendencies should structured feedback on teaching help overcome?
options: Speaking too fast and too quietly
Focusing only on content (though delivery matters as much) and giving only negative or only positive feedback
pool.explain: Balanced feedback on content and delivery is the most useful.
pool.evidence: This helps overcome two common tendencies when giving feedback on teaching: to focus on the content (even though delivery is at least as important) and to either provide only negative or only positive feedback.

pool.q: What mindset does assuming teaching is an innate talent reflect?
pool.explain: Teaching, like other skills, improves with practice and feedback.
pool.evidence: or innate skill is to take on a fixed mindset about teaching

pool.q: How does the lesson suggest instructors improve their teaching?
options: Through peer-to-peer lesson practice with feedback
pool.explain: Feedback should cover delivery as well as content.
pool.evidence: Use peer-to-peer lesson practice to transform your instruction.

pool.q: What does live coding force the instructor to do?
pool.explain: Going at typing speed gives learners time to follow along.
pool.evidence: Live coding forces the instructor to slow down.

pool.q: How is participatory live coding different from teaching from a slide deck?
options: A slide deck is like a railway track; live coding lets instructors go off-road and follow learners' interests
pool.explain: Learners also see how experts deal with mistakes.
pool.evidence: Where a slide deck is like a railway track, participatory live coding allows instructors to go off-road and follow their learners' interests.

pool.q: What is arguably the most important outcome an instructor can achieve?
options: Covering every topic in the lesson
Cultivating learners' motivation to continue learning
pool.explain: Motivated learners keep building the skill after the workshop.
pool.evidence: cultivating motivation to continue learning, and to carefully pursue best-practices in doing so, is arguably the most important outcome we can achieve

pool.q: How can you counter learners' doubts about whether a lesson is useful?
options: Start with something quick to learn and immediately useful
pool.explain: Early wins build motivation.
pool.evidence: begin a lesson with something that is quick to learn and immediately useful

pool.q: What must any useful estimate of time saved account for?
options: Only the time to type commands
How often failures happen and how much time they cost
pool.explain: Real time includes debugging and recovering from mistakes.
pool.evidence: Any useful estimate of time must take into account how frequent failures are and how much time is lost to them.

pool.q: What influences learner motivation beyond the instructor's control?
pool.explain: Instructors can still avoid demotivating learners.
pool.evidence: learner motivation is influenced by many factors well beyond the control of an instructor, including individual background and systemic forces

pool.q: What does accessibility support (accommodations) mean?
options: Making a lesson shorter for everyone
Changing things to serve an individual with a demonstrated need
pool.explain: Universal design goes further, building accessibility in for everyone from the start.
pool.evidence: Accessibility support means changing things to serve an individual with a demonstrated need (also known as accommodations).

pool.q: What is the key to Universal Design for Learning (UDL)?
options: Redundancy, so learners have several ways to receive, engage with and share information
Teaching every learner exactly the same way
pool.explain: UDL designs for everyone rather than adjusting for individuals later.
pool.evidence: The key to UDL is creating redundancies such that learners have multiple options

pool.q: Which quick changes can make a workshop more accessible?
options: Good font choices and text size, and checking step-free access to the room
pool.explain: Many accessibility steps are quick and cheap.
pool.evidence: font choices, text size, checking in advance that your room is accessible via an elevator or ramp

pool.q: What is one of the greatest strengths of Carpentries workshops?
options: They are prepared and run by more than one person
pool.explain: Never teach alone: helpers support learners while the instructor teaches.
pool.evidence: workshops are prepared and executed by more than one person.

pool.q: During live coding or demonstration, what should learners be doing?
pool.explain: Participation turns watching into practice.
pool.evidence: your learners should be actively working along with you wherever possible

pool.q: What does the lesson say about two-day workshops?
options: They are too short to learn anything
pool.explain: Plan breaks and support accordingly.
pool.evidence: two day workshops are intense

pool.q: Will you ever know everything about the learners in your classroom?
options: No — it helps to recognise that you never will
pool.explain: Still, learner profiles help you anticipate needs.
pool.evidence: it is useful to recognise that you will never know everything about the individuals who come into your classroom

pool.q: What are Carpentries lesson objectives usually like?
options: Specific about what a learner should be able to do by the end
pool.explain: Specific, observable actions make objectives checkable.
pool.evidence: In most cases they are quite specific about what a learner should be able to do by the end of the episode.

pool.q: Which reference does the lesson recommend for judging the 'level' of a learning task?
pool.explain: It ranks tasks from remembering to creating.
pool.evidence: we recommend having a look at one of many excellent references on Bloom's Taxonomy

pool.q: Which instruments help Carpentries instructors plan and understand their workshop?
pool.explain: Surveys reveal learners' backgrounds before you teach.
pool.evidence: The Carpentries strives to create useful assessment instruments that can help you plan and understand your workshop

pool.q: Why make a plan for using the teaching practices you have learned?
options: It makes it easier to remember to use them
Plans are required to get paid
pool.explain: Some practices happen at particular points; others throughout.
pool.evidence: Having a plan makes it easier for you to remember to implement the important teaching practices you have learned.

pool.q: Is there a right answer when organising your teaching knowledge into categories?
options: No — it's about building your own mental model
pool.explain: You are moving from novice towards competent practitioner.
pool.evidence: this is about you building up a mental model
